case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Title VII’s requirement that employers reasonably accommodate an employee’s religious practice unless it would cause an “undue hardship” should continue to be governed by the low threshold from Trans World Airlines, Inc. v. Hardison (more than a de minimis cost) or instead require a materially greater showing of burden on the employer’s business.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a) (religious discrimination) and § 2000e(j) (definition of “religion” and duty of “reasonable accommodation” absent “undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Groff argues that the Third Circuit applied an overly employer-friendly standard derived from Hardison—treating “undue hardship” as anything imposing more than a de minimis cost—and that this reading is inconsistent with Title VII’s text, structure, and ordinary meaning of “undue hardship.” He contends that an employer should have to show a substantially greater, business-significant burden (not merely coworker dissatisfaction, administrative inconvenience, or routine schedule reshuffling) before denying a religious accommodation; on that proper standard, USPS should have been required to accommodate his Sunday Sabbath observance through scheduling adjustments, voluntary shift swaps, or other operational measures.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Postmaster General/USPS argues that existing Supreme Court precedent (Hardison) already defines Title VII’s undue-hardship standard, that the Third Circuit correctly applied it, and that USPS did provide and attempt accommodations but ultimately faced undue hardship from repeatedly exempting Groff from Sunday work in a delivery environment increasingly requiring Sunday staffing (notably for Amazon deliveries). USPS emphasizes the concrete operational and workforce impacts—difficulty staffing required Sunday routes, burdens shifted to other employees, workplace disruption, and potential effects on service reliability—and maintains that Title VII does not require accommodations that impose more than minimal costs or that compromise core operational needs.
key_precedents: Trans World Airlines, Inc. v. Hardison (1977)
Ansonia Board of Education v. Philbrook (1986)
Employment Division v. Smith (1990) (often discussed for contrast in religious-protection frameworks, though not a Title VII case)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—stare decisis plus congressional inaction—is real, but under my minimalist approach it cannot justify perpetuating a gloss that sits uncomfortably with § 2000e(j)’s text (“undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business”), especially when Hardison is fairly read as driven by the seniority-system/operational-disruption facts rather than a freestanding “any nontrivial cost” rule. As Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett emphasize, we can preserve reliance interests by retaining Hardison’s core holdings (no duty to breach bona fide seniority systems; no duty to incur material operational burdens) while clarifying that trivial costs, administrative friction, or coworker resentment untethered to business impact are not “undue hardship.” Ansonia does not cut the other way; its “reasonable accommodation” principle presupposes a meaningful hardship inquiry once accommodation options are on the table, and the Third Circuit’s approach collapses that inquiry into something too thin to square with the statute. A narrow clarification along these lines best protects the Court’s institutional legitimacy without unsettling settled results where genuine business disruption is shown.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—stare decisis and congressional inaction—cannot justify retaining Hardison’s “more than a de minimis cost” formulation where it conflicts with the enacted text: “undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business” (and the ordinary public meaning of “undue”) demands a substantial, not trivial, burden. Under an originalist and textualist approach, Congress’s failure to amend does not ratify a judicial rewrite; at most it shows legislative inertia, especially when the precedent’s gloss is atextual. As Justice Gorsuch notes, continuing to apply the de minimis test effectively reads “undue” out of § 2000e(j), and we can preserve Hardison’s seniority-system holding, as the Chief Justice suggests, without converting routine scheduling friction or coworker dissatisfaction into “undue hardship.” Ansonia Bd. of Educ. v. Philbrook does not rescue the de minimis standard; it presupposes a meaningful undue-hardship inquiry once a reasonable accommodation is identified, rather than collapsing that inquiry into any nontrivial inconvenience.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I take the Chief Justice’s and Justice Thomas’s textual point seriously: “undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business” is not naturally read to mean any slight burden. But as Chief Justice Roberts himself acknowledges, Hardison can be understood as focusing on concrete operational burdens and seniority-system constraints, and in the scheduling context that often cashes out as the employer not being required to absorb more than minimal (and recurring) disruptions to coverage and costs—precisely the sort of business-conduct impacts Hardison addressed. Justice Kagan’s concern about lower courts treating “coworker resentment” as dispositive is fair, yet the Third Circuit’s analysis here (as I read the record) rested on operational impacts and the redistribution of work in a way that affects service and staffing, not mere offense or grumbling. Given decades of reliance and Congress’s choice not to revise § 2000e(j), I do not think the text-based discomfort with Hardison’s shorthand is sufficient to warrant recalibrating the governing standard in a way that invites uncertainty and new litigation over line-drawing.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s stare decisis/congressional-acquiescence point is the strongest for Respondent, but it cannot justify entrenching a gloss that effectively reads “undue” out of “undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business,” especially given the predictable real-world consequence of shifting accommodation costs onto low-power religious employees. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts’s narrow path: preserve Hardison’s core holding where a bona fide seniority system or concrete operational disruption is shown, while rejecting any rule that lets trivial costs, coworker resentment, or routine scheduling friction suffice. Ansonia, as Justice Kagan notes, confirms employers need not provide the employee’s preferred accommodation, but it presupposes a meaningful undue-hardship threshold—so it does not rescue the Third Circuit’s “any nontrivial cost” approach. Under my pragmatic, fairness-focused methodology, the statute is best implemented by requiring a business-significant showing of hardship rather than allowing inconvenience to defeat accommodation.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s stare decisis/reliance point is the hardest issue, but it doesn’t justify perpetuating a “de minimis” formulation that sits uneasily with Congress’s words—“undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business”—which naturally connotes a meaningful, business-focused burden. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, we can preserve Hardison’s core results (especially the seniority-system holding and the recognition that material operational disruption can be undue) while clarifying that trivial costs, routine administrative friction, or bare coworker resentment are not enough. Justice Barrett’s point that poor textual fit diminishes precedential weight is persuasive under my pragmatic textualism: an administrable standard should track the enacted phrase “undue hardship” and avoid a threshold that effectively collapses the accommodation duty. Ansonia’s “reasonable accommodation” framework still leaves employers flexibility, but it presupposes a real undue-hardship inquiry rather than a shortcut that treats any nontrivial cost as dispositive.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s stare decisis and congressional-acquiescence argument is the strongest case for affirmance, but under my textualist methodology it cannot justify retaining a judge-made “de minimis” threshold that dilutes Congress’s word “undue” in “undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business.” As Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas emphasize, ordinary meaning points to a substantial or excessive burden tied to business operations, and that reading can preserve Hardison’s core holding about bona fide seniority systems without freezing in place its most atextual phrasing. The Chief Justice’s point about Ansonia is also important: it presupposes a real undue-hardship inquiry after a reasonable accommodation is identified, not a shortcut where routine inconvenience or coworker resentment ends the analysis. Reliance interests do not trump the enacted text where the precedent’s gloss has become detached from that text; the proper course is clarification rather than perpetuation.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s stare decisis and congressional-acquiescence point is the strongest counterweight, but it is diminished where Hardison’s oft-quoted “de minimis” gloss is in substantial tension with the statutory text requiring an “undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business.” I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that we can preserve Hardison’s concrete holdings—especially the bona fide seniority-system and genuine operational-disruption contexts—while clarifying that trivial costs, routine administrative friction, or bare coworker resentment (untethered to business operations) do not suffice. Justice Kagan’s administrability concern reinforces this: the Third Circuit’s “any nontrivial cost” approach collapses the statutory inquiry and invites outcomes disconnected from “undue” and from “the conduct of the employer’s business.” Ansonia, as Roberts notes, does not rescue the de minimis standard; it presupposes a meaningful undue-hardship backstop once a reasonable accommodation is identified, and our job is to realign that backstop with the statute while respecting legitimate reliance interests.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—stare decisis plus congressional inaction—deserves careful weight, but it cannot justify retaining an interpretive shorthand that sits uneasily with § 2000e(j)’s enacted phrase “undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business,” which in ordinary public meaning requires a materially burdensome impact rather than any more-than-trivial cost. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, we can respect reliance interests by preserving Hardison’s core holdings (especially the seniority-system principle and the rejection of accommodations that significantly disrupt operations) while clarifying that coworker resentment or routine administrative inconvenience, without demonstrated business-significant effects, is not “undue hardship.” Justice Alito is right that scheduling exemptions can impose real operational costs, but that observation supports a properly business-focused “undue hardship” inquiry rather than a de minimis threshold that risks reading “undue” out of the statute. Ansonia’s reasonable-accommodation framework remains intact under this approach because it presupposes a meaningful hardship backstop tied to the employer’s business, not a trivial-cost shortcut.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s stare decisis and reliance argument deserves respect, but it is not enough to preserve a “de minimis” gloss that sits uneasily with § 2000e(j)’s text and has, in practice, drained the accommodation duty of meaningful content. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan suggest, we can honor reliance interests by reading Hardison in light of its concrete operational-disruption and bona fide seniority-system setting, while clarifying that routine scheduling friction, marginal costs, or coworker resentment (without demonstrated impact on the conduct of the business) are not “undue hardship.” Ansonia, which Alito invokes, does not cure the problem because it presupposes a real undue-hardship inquiry; it merely confirms employers need not provide the employee’s preferred accommodation once a reasonable one is available. On a pragmatic, fairness-centered approach, a business-significant burden standard better aligns with statutory language and administrability without compelling accommodations that genuinely disrupt operations.

John Roberts.reasoning: Title VII defines “religion” to include practices that an employer must accommodate unless doing so would impose an “undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j), and the ordinary meaning of “undue hardship” connotes a substantial, not minimal, burden. Hardison’s “more than a de minimis cost” phrasing has proved unmoored from the statute’s text and can be read as an overbroad gloss tied to that case’s particular concern with disrupting a seniority system, rather than a universal, low-threshold rule. Consistent with institutional legitimacy and stare decisis, the better course is a narrow clarification: retain Hardison’s core holding that Title VII does not require accommodations that impose significant operational burdens or violate legitimate seniority systems, while rejecting any interpretation that treats trivial costs or generalized coworker resentment as “undue hardship.” Ansonia Bd. of Educ. v. Philbrook confirms that “reasonable accommodation” is context-specific and does not require the employee’s preferred option, but it presupposes a meaningful “undue hardship” inquiry—one focused on material burdens to the employer’s business, not de minimis expense.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Title VII’s text requires accommodation unless the employer shows “undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j); read in ordinary public meaning, “undue hardship” denotes a substantial, not trivial, burden. Hardison’s “more than a de minimis cost” gloss is difficult to square with that statutory language and effectively rewrites “undue” out of the statute, so stare decisis carries less weight where precedent departs from the enacted text. Properly construed, burdens that fall only as coworker resentment or routine administrative inconvenience do not, without more, establish “undue hardship” on the business itself. I would therefore disapprove Hardison’s de minimis formulation and require a materially greater showing consistent with § 2000e(j)’s text.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Title VII requires accommodation only so long as it does not impose an “undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j), and this Court in Trans World Airlines, Inc. v. Hardison interpreted that limitation to mean an employer need not bear more than a de minimis cost, particularly where accommodations would disrupt scheduling and impose burdens on operations. Whatever academic criticism exists of Hardison’s phrasing, it has functioned as the governing standard for decades, and stare decisis carries special force where Congress has left that interpretation undisturbed. On the facts presented, repeatedly excusing an employee from Sunday work in a delivery operation with increasing Sunday staffing requirements predictably shifts work to others and risks service disruption—practical consequences that fall squarely within “the conduct of the employer’s business.” Accordingly, the Third Circuit did not err in applying Hardison rather than adopting a materially more demanding test.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Title VII defines “religion” to include “all aspects of religious observance and practice” unless the employer shows it “is unable to reasonably accommodate … without undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j), and the ordinary meaning of “undue hardship” requires a materially significant burden, not merely “more than a de minimis cost.” Hardison’s “de minimis” phrasing is not compelled by the statutory text and has operated in practice to dilute Congress’s protection and to shift the costs of accommodation onto religious employees—often those with the least workplace power—contrary to Title VII’s remedial purpose. Consistent with Ansonia Board of Education v. Philbrook (1986), the inquiry should focus on whether the employer has offered a reasonable accommodation and whether denying the requested one is justified by genuine hardship to the business, not generalized coworker resentment or routine scheduling inconvenience. On that understanding, USPS must show a substantial, business-significant hardship from accommodating Sunday Sabbath observance rather than relying on minimal administrative or staffing friction.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Title VII’s text requires accommodation unless the employer shows “undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j), and ordinary meaning suggests a substantial, not trifling, burden; the “more than a de minimis cost” phrase in Hardison sits uneasily with that language and has proven difficult to administer coherently. A pragmatic, workable reading preserves Hardison’s core point that Title VII does not require accommodations that meaningfully disrupt operations or violate neutral seniority systems, but clarifies that “undue hardship” demands a materially greater showing tied to the employer’s business rather than generalized coworker resentment. Ansonia Bd. of Educ. v. Philbrook confirms that employers need only offer a reasonable accommodation, yet the reasonableness inquiry must be anchored to § 2000e(j)’s “undue hardship” limit, which calls for a real, business-significant burden. Because the Third Circuit treated minimal costs and routine scheduling frictions as sufficient, I would vote to disapprove the de minimis gloss and require a higher, business-focused threshold.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Title VII commands “reasonable accommodation” for religious exercise unless the employer demonstrates “undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j), and the ordinary meaning of “undue hardship” requires a showing of a substantial—not trivial—burden. Hardison’s “more than a de minimis cost” formulation is difficult to square with the statutory text and appears to be, at most, an atextual gloss that cannot override Congress’s chosen words. Respect for separation of powers counsels that courts apply the statute as written rather than perpetuate a judge-made standard that effectively rewrites “undue” to mean “any.” Accordingly, the Third Circuit’s reliance on Hardison’s de minimis threshold should be rejected in favor of a materially greater showing of hardship on the employer’s business.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Title VII requires “reasonable accommodation” of religious practice unless it would impose an “undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j), and the ordinary meaning of “undue hardship” suggests a substantial burden, not merely a minimal or trifling one. Hardison’s “more than a de minimis cost” formulation has proven difficult to square with the statutory text and has generated an unduly employer-friendly rule that risks turning a textual protection into a near-nullity, while still allowing employers to deny accommodations that materially impair operations. Consistent with precedent and judicial restraint, the Court should not discard Hardison wholesale, but should clarify that undue hardship requires a meaningful, business-significant burden rather than coworker resentment or routine administrative inconvenience. That approach better fits Title VII’s text and preserves a workable standard while respecting reliance interests by focusing the inquiry on concrete effects on the employer’s business.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Title VII defines “religion” to include religious “practice” that an employer must “reasonably accommodate” unless it would impose an “undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business.” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j). Textually, “undue hardship” connotes a substantial or excessive burden, not merely “more than a de minimis cost,” and Hardison’s oft-quoted formulation is difficult to reconcile with the statute’s ordinary meaning and focus on hardship to the employer’s business rather than generalized inconvenience or coworker resentment. While precedent matters, Hardison can be read to require a showing tied to meaningful business burdens (and to avoid accommodations that violate a bona fide seniority system), without perpetuating a de minimis gloss untethered to § 2000e(j)’s text; Ansonia Bd. of Educ. v. Philbrook likewise confirms that the inquiry turns on the reasonableness of the accommodation and the presence of undue hardship. Accordingly, I would vote to reject the de minimis threshold and require a materially greater showing of burden on the employer’s business before denying a religious accommodation.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Title VII’s text requires accommodation unless the employer shows “undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j), and the ordinary meaning of “undue” demands a materially greater burden than the “more than a de minimis cost” formulation often attributed to Hardison. Hardison, 432 U.S. 63 (1977), is best read as addressing a specific seniority-system and collective-bargaining context and should not be extended into a broad, employer-friendly rule that effectively collapses “undue hardship” into “any nontrivial inconvenience,” undermining procedural fairness for religious employees. A pragmatic, consequence-sensitive reading of § 2000e(j) should focus on concrete, business-significant operational costs—not generalized coworker resentment or routine scheduling friction—consistent with Title VII’s accommodation structure and this Court’s direction that an employer must offer a reasonable accommodation rather than the employee’s preferred one, see Ansonia Bd. of Educ. v. Philbrook (1986). Applying that more faithful standard here, USPS should have been required to show a substantial burden on its business operations, not merely marginal costs or redistributed work, before denying Groff’s Sabbath accommodation.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Title VII’s requirement that employers reasonably accommodate an employee’s religious observance allows an employer to deny an accommodation whenever it would impose anything more than a minimal cost (“more than de minimis”), or instead requires showing a substantially greater hardship before refusing the accommodation.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(a) (religious discrimination) and § 2000e(j) (definition of “religion” including a duty to accommodate unless the employer demonstrates “undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Groff argues that the Court should reject/clarify the long-applied “more than de minimis” undue-hardship standard derived from TWA v. Hardison because it improperly waters down Title VII’s text (“undue hardship”) and leaves religious employees with little real protection; he contends USPS could have accommodated his Sunday Sabbath observance through scheduling adjustments without the kind of significant business disruption that qualifies as an “undue hardship,” and that impacts such as coworker grumbling or routine administrative burdens should not suffice to deny accommodation.
case_analysis.respondent_position: USPS argues that existing Supreme Court precedent (especially Hardison) already sets the governing rule and the lower courts properly applied it; it contends accommodating Groff’s refusal to work Sundays required shifting his work to other employees and/or creating operational shortfalls, harming service reliability and workplace operations, and that Title VII does not require an employer to impose those burdens—particularly when accommodation would materially affect other workers or the employer’s ability to run its business—so denial of the requested accommodation was lawful under the established undue-hardship framework.
key_precedents: Trans World Airlines, Inc. v. Hardison (1977)
Ansonia Board of Education v. Philbrook (1986)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s stare decisis and reliance argument is the most serious obstacle, but it proves too much: reliance attaches to Hardison’s core holding that Title VII does not compel accommodations that impose genuine hardship on business operations or require breaching a bona fide seniority system, not to preserving the “more than de minimis” phrase as a freestanding rule that dilutes the statutory word “undue.” Justice Kavanaugh’s approach offers the narrow, legitimacy-preserving path—retain Hardison’s result and its seniority-system principle, while clarifying that “undue hardship” means a substantial increased cost or significant operational disruption in the overall context of the employer’s business, and that coworker impacts matter only insofar as they translate into concrete business burdens. Ansonia, as Justice Kagan notes, fits comfortably with that clarification because it addresses the employer’s latitude to choose among reasonable accommodations, not a license to deny accommodations based on trivial costs. On that clarified standard, the court below applied the wrong measure by treating minimal burdens as dispositive, so vacatur and remand remain appropriate.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s stare decisis and congressional-acquiescence argument does not overcome the statutory text: § 2000e(j) asks whether the accommodation imposes an “undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business,” and a “more than de minimis” rule effectively deletes “undue” from the enacted standard. Under an originalist, textualist approach, we owe the greatest fidelity to the ordinary public meaning of the words Congress enacted, and when a precedent’s verbal formula departs from that meaning, its stare decisis weight is diminished. As Justice Kavanaugh and the Chief Justice propose, we can respect Hardison’s core holding (especially regarding bona fide seniority systems) while clarifying that undue hardship requires a materially significant cost or disruption to business operations; coworker impacts matter only insofar as they translate into such business burdens. Justice Alito’s reliance on Ansonia does not alter that conclusion because Ansonia concerns whether an offered accommodation is reasonable, not a license to dilute the separate “undue hardship” threshold below what the text can bear.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I take seriously the Chief Justice’s and Justice Barrett’s ordinary-meaning point that “undue hardship” connotes something more weighty than a trivial burden, but Hardison is not just a stray phrase—it is a longstanding operational construction that Congress has left in place and that employers have relied upon in structuring workplace rules and scheduling systems. Justice Kavanaugh’s suggested “clarify-not-overrule” approach still, in practice, invites courts to relitigate what counts as “substantial” in a way that destabilizes administrable lines and discounts the very real operational consequences of predictable scheduling gaps in essential services like USPS. Hardison and Ansonia together already contain limiting principles: the employer must offer a reasonable accommodation, but it need not accept accommodations that impose real workplace inefficiencies, disrupt operations, or shift burdens in ways that impair service—those are hardships on the conduct of the business. On this record, excusing Sunday work foreseeably shifted work and risked shortfalls; that is precisely the kind of business-linked hardship Hardison treated as sufficient, so I would affirm.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s stare decisis and reliance argument deserves respect, but it cannot lock in a “more than de minimis” gloss that effectively reads “undue” out of § 2000e(j) and has predictably displaced accommodation burdens onto employees least able to bear them. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh explain, we can honor Hardison’s core holding—especially its refusal to require violations of bona fide seniority systems—while clarifying that undue hardship requires a substantial, business-linked burden, not routine scheduling friction or coworker resentment untethered from operational disruption. Ansonia, which several colleagues invoke, strengthens administrability by confirming the employer need not provide the employee’s preferred accommodation, but it does not authorize denying accommodation based on trivial costs. On this record, the lower court’s de minimis framing prematurely ended the statutory inquiry and warrants vacatur and remand under the clarified standard.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s stare decisis/reliance argument is the most serious obstacle, but it ultimately does not require preserving Hardison’s “more than de minimis” phrase as a controlling legal standard when § 2000e(j) says “undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business.” As the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh stress, we can honor Hardison’s core holding—especially its protection for bona fide seniority systems—while clarifying that “undue” demands a substantial, business-linked burden rather than ordinary scheduling friction or coworker resentment untethered to operations. Ansonia, which several colleagues invoke, actually supports administrability under that clarification because it lets employers choose among reasonable accommodations; it does not license lowering the hardship threshold below what the text can bear. The judgment below should be vacated because its de minimis framing short-circuited the statutory inquiry into whether USPS faced a genuinely undue hardship in the overall context of its business.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s stare decisis and reliance point deserves respect, but it cannot justify preserving a verbal formula that effectively deletes “undue” from § 2000e(j); when precedent’s gloss departs from enacted text, its gravitational pull is reduced under an originalist and textualist method. I find the Chief Justice’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s approach most consistent with that duty: treat Hardison’s “more than de minimis” phrase as an imprecise shorthand tied to its seniority-system facts, while clarifying that “undue hardship” requires a materially significant cost or operational disruption to the business—not ordinary scheduling friction or coworker displeasure untethered to business impact. Ansonia, as Justice Kagan notes, affects the analysis only by confirming employers may choose among reasonable accommodations; it does not license a diminished hardship threshold. On that clarified standard, the decision below should be vacated and remanded because it treated minimal costs as dispositive rather than applying the statutory “undue hardship” inquiry in context.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s stare decisis and reliance argument remains the strongest point for Respondent, but I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that any reliance interests attach to Hardison’s core holding (especially its seniority-system and genuine operational-burden concerns), not to preserving the “more than de minimis” phrase as a freestanding, atextual rule. As Justice Kagan notes, § 2000e(j)’s enacted language—“undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business”—cannot naturally be read to mean any nontrivial cost, and retaining that gloss has invited denials based on trivial burdens, which undermines coherence and legitimacy. Ansonia, cited by Justices Thomas and Kagan, supports an administrable approach: employers may choose among reasonable accommodations, but must show a substantial, business-linked burden to deny accommodation—coworker impacts matter only insofar as they translate into concrete operational costs or significant disruption. That path respects precedent without overruling Hardison wholesale, and it warrants vacatur and remand where the lower court treated minimal cost as dispositive.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito is right to stress stare decisis, congressional inaction, and employer reliance on Hardison’s long-settled framework, and we should be cautious about unsettling settled expectations. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh explain, the reliance interest is best understood as attaching to Hardison’s core holding (including its protection for bona fide seniority systems and refusal to require accommodations imposing genuine business disruption), not to the “more than de minimis” phrase when it functions as a freestanding rule that collapses “undue hardship” into triviality and thus departs from § 2000e(j)’s text. Ansonia, which Justice Alito invokes, does not rescue the de minimis gloss; it addresses whether an offered accommodation is reasonable and confirms employer choice among reasonable options, but it does not authorize lowering the statutory threshold for “undue hardship.” Under an original public meaning approach attentive to precedent, the better course is to clarify that undue hardship requires a substantial burden on the conduct of the employer’s business, with coworker impacts relevant only insofar as they translate into concrete operational costs or significant disruption.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point remains stare decisis and congressional acquiescence, but under my pragmatic, fairness-focused approach those considerations cannot entrench an atextual rule that predictably permits denial of religious accommodations based on trivial burdens and thereby skews against minority faith practices. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh argue, we can respect reliance interests by preserving Hardison’s core holding (especially its protection for bona fide seniority systems) while clarifying that “undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business” requires a materially significant, business-linked burden—so coworker impacts count only when they translate into concrete operational disruption or substantial cost. Justice Kagan’s point about how lower courts have treated “more than de minimis” as dispositive underscores the practical consequence: the gloss has functioned as a systematic underenforcement of a civil-rights protection, which weakens stare decisis weight where the precedent’s reasoning is thin. Ansonia, as several colleagues note, makes the clarified standard workable because employers may choose among reasonable accommodations; they just must justify denial with genuine undue hardship rather than routine scheduling friction.

John Roberts.reasoning: Title VII defines “religion” to include a duty to accommodate religious observance unless the employer shows “undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j), and the statutory phrase naturally connotes a substantial, not trifling, burden. Although Trans World Airlines, Inc. v. Hardison has long been read to allow denial for any accommodation imposing “more than a de minimis cost,” that formulation is best understood as an imprecise gloss rather than a necessary holding, and it has produced atextual results that erode Title VII’s protection while inviting extensive litigation. To preserve institutional legitimacy and respect precedent without overruling more than necessary, the Court should retain Hardison’s bottom-line principle that employers need not bear undue burdens, but clarify that “undue hardship” requires a showing of substantial increased costs or significant disruption to the business, not mere coworker unhappiness or ordinary administrative inconvenience. On that clarified standard, Groff is entitled at least to reconsideration of whether USPS demonstrated undue hardship on its business operations.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Title VII’s text requires accommodation unless the employer shows “undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j); the ordinary public meaning of “undue hardship” denotes a substantial, not trivial, burden. Hardison’s “more than de minimis cost” gloss, 432 U.S. 63, 84 (1977), lacks a persuasive textual anchor and effectively rewrites “undue” out of the statute, so stare decisis carries less force where precedent departs from the enacted text. Ansonia Board of Education v. Philbrook, 479 U.S. 60 (1986), confirms the statutory duty is one of “reasonable accommodation” subject only to a properly understood “undue hardship,” not mere coworker dissatisfaction or routine administrative inconvenience. Because the statute places the burden on the employer to demonstrate undue hardship, USPS must show a materially significant disruption to its business operations, not simply any marginal added cost.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Title VII defines “religion” to include an employer’s duty to accommodate only so long as the employer does not incur “undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j), and this Court in Trans World Airlines, Inc. v. Hardison interpreted that language to permit denial where the accommodation would impose more than a de minimis cost. Respect for stare decisis is especially warranted where Congress has left Hardison’s construction in place for decades and employers have structured operations in reliance on it. Here, requiring USPS to exempt an employee from Sunday work predictably shifted burdens to other employees and risked service shortfalls, consequences Hardison recognized as sufficient hardship when they implicate operational efficiency and workplace functioning. While the statutory phrase “undue hardship” is not self-defining, Hardison and Ansonia Board of Education v. Philbrook confirm that Title VII does not compel accommodations that materially disrupt the employer’s business or impose more than minimal costs.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Title VII defines “religion” to require reasonable accommodation unless the employer shows “undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j), and that statutory text demands more than the “more than de minimis cost” gloss drawn from Hardison. Hardison’s phrasing was not anchored in the ordinary meaning of “undue hardship,” and its emphasis on collective-bargaining constraints and coworker burden should not be treated as dispositive when the employer can mitigate impacts through scheduling, voluntary swaps, or other workplace adjustments without substantial disruption. Denying accommodation based on routine administrative costs or coworker dissatisfaction risks forcing vulnerable workers to choose between faith and employment—precisely what Congress sought to prevent—while a “substantial hardship” standard better balances religious equality with legitimate business needs. Ansonia Bd. of Educ. v. Philbrook confirms employers need not provide the employee’s preferred accommodation, but it does not justify reducing “undue hardship” to minimal inconvenience.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Title VII’s text requires accommodation unless the employer demonstrates an “undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j), and “undue hardship” does not naturally mean any burden “more than de minimis.” Hardison’s “more than de minimis cost” phrasing is best read as an overbroad gloss untethered from the statute’s language and has proved insufficiently workable because it allows routine administrative burdens or coworker resentment to defeat accommodations without a meaningful showing of hardship to the business. Consistent with § 2000e(j) and with Ansonia Bd. of Educ. v. Philbrook’s focus on providing a “reasonable accommodation” (without requiring the employee’s preferred one), the proper standard is that the employer must show a substantial burden in the overall context of its business, not trivial costs. On that understanding, USPS must do more than point to ordinary scheduling friction or generalized impacts on coworkers to deny accommodation.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Title VII’s text requires an employer to “reasonably accommodate” religious observance unless it can show “undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j), and the ordinary meaning of “undue hardship” demands more than a trifling or minimal cost. Hardison’s “more than de minimis” phrasing is difficult to square with the statute’s language and appears, at most, an imprecise gloss rather than a faithful construction of § 2000e(j)’s standard, especially where the decision turned on the interaction with a seniority system. Respect for Congress’s words and separation-of-powers principles counsels against letting judicial embellishment displace the enacted text, and any residual ambiguity in a rule exposing employees to liability-like burdens should not be resolved to dilute statutory protection. Accordingly, the employer must show a substantially greater hardship than minimal expense or coworker displeasure before denying a religious accommodation.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Title VII defines “religion” to require reasonable accommodation unless the employer shows “undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j), and that text, read in ordinary usage and in historical context, demands more than a merely minimal (“de minimis”) burden. Hardison’s “more than de minimis cost” formulation is best understood as an imprecise gloss tied to the particular facts there (including a collectively bargained seniority system) rather than a faithful, generally applicable interpretation of § 2000e(j)’s “undue hardship” standard, and the Court should clarify the governing rule to better align with the statute while retaining the core holding that Title VII does not require violating bona fide seniority systems. A workable standard is that an employer must show a substantial burden in the overall context of its business operations; impacts on coworkers matter only insofar as they translate into concrete operational costs or disruptions to the business itself, consistent with Ansonia Bd. of Educ. v. Philbrook’s approach to “reasonable accommodation.” This course respects precedent by narrowing and clarifying Hardison rather than overruling its essential result, while restoring coherence to Title VII’s text and ensuring administrable, practical guidance for employers and employees.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 2000e(j) excuses an employer from providing a religious accommodation only upon a showing of “undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business,” and the ordinary public meaning of “undue hardship” connotes a substantial burden, not any cost above a trivial (“de minimis”) one. The “more than de minimis” phrase in Trans World Airlines, Inc. v. Hardison, 432 U.S. 63, 84 (1977), is best read as an imprecise gloss that cannot be squared with the statute’s text and therefore should be clarified to require a materially greater showing, while still respecting Hardison’s core holding that Title VII does not compel accommodations that impose substantial costs or violate bona fide seniority systems. Ansonia Bd. of Educ. v. Philbrook, 479 U.S. 60 (1986), confirms the employer’s duty is to provide a reasonable accommodation, not the employee’s preferred one, but it does not justify diluting “undue hardship” below its textual threshold. Accordingly, I would vote to reject the de minimis standard and require the employer to demonstrate a substantial burden on business operations before denying accommodation.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Title VII’s text defines “religion” to require reasonable accommodation unless the employer demonstrates “undue hardship on the conduct of the employer’s business,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(j), and “undue” connotes a materially significant burden—not any cost above “de minimis.” The “more than de minimis cost” formulation associated with Trans World Airlines, Inc. v. Hardison (1977) is in tension with the statute’s language and risks systematically underprotecting religious employees, particularly minorities, by making denial too easy based on routine administrative burdens or coworker dissatisfaction. Consistent with procedural fairness and practical consequences, I would clarify that an employer must show a substantially greater hardship tied to business operations (not merely impacts on coworkers untethered to business conduct) before refusing accommodation, while still recognizing, as Hardison emphasized, that Title VII does not require violating bona fide seniority systems. Because the lower court treated minimal cost as dispositive rather than applying a genuinely “undue hardship” inquiry, I would vote to reverse and remand under the corrected standard.
